text: You already write joins the same way on every platform you've touched so far in this course — T-SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. This lesson introduces the one exception in this entire catalog of dialects: Oracle, which carries a second, older way to write an outer join that none of the other three platforms ever had. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to read it, even though you'll never need to write it yourself.

Here's the ANSI syntax you already know, cold: FROM Orders, LEFT JOIN Customers, ON o dot CustomerID equals c dot CustomerID. The join type and the join condition sit together in the FROM clause, right next to each other. T-SQL has never had any other way to write this. Neither has MySQL. Neither has PostgreSQL. ANSI join syntax is the only syntax those three platforms have ever supported — there's no legacy alternative to unlearn on any of them.

Oracle is different. Before Oracle implemented ANSI join syntax, outer joins were written by putting a plus sign in parentheses next to a column, inside the WHERE clause — not the FROM clause. FROM orders o, customers c, WHERE o dot customer id equals c dot customer id, open paren, plus, close paren. That plus sign marks which side of the comparison is allowed to have no matching row. Here it's on the customers side, so every order shows up even when it has no matching customer — the same result you'd get from a LEFT JOIN. You'll still run into this in Oracle code written before the early 2000s. It's legacy, not current best practice, but it's real, and you need to recognize it when you see it.

Here's why ANSI syntax won, with a concrete example. Try to put the plus sign on BOTH sides of a comparison, to express a full outer join, and Oracle throws error ORA-01468 — it's simply illegal. The old syntax has no way to say 'show me unmatched rows from either side.' ANSI syntax handles that directly: FULL OUTER JOIN customers c, ON o dot customer id equals c dot customer id. No workaround needed. That's one real, concrete limitation of the old syntax, not just a style preference.

There's a second limitation that matters even more in practice: once a query joins three or more tables, every join condition using the old syntax lives together in one flat WHERE clause. It becomes easy to apply the plus sign inconsistently across tables and get an ambiguous or outright wrong result. ANSI syntax avoids this because each join keyword carries its own ON condition right next to it — the join graph stays readable and unambiguous no matter how many tables you add. That's exactly why Oracle itself now recommends ANSI syntax, even on Oracle. The practical rule for this entire course: write ANSI joins everywhere, on every platform, including Oracle. The only reason to recognize the old syntax at all is to read someone else's legacy code, not to write your own.

To recap: Oracle is the one dialect here with a legacy outer-join operator living in the WHERE clause; it can't directly express a full outer join, and it gets harder to reason about as more tables join in. T-SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL never had this quirk to begin with. Next lesson, we look at a case where the dialects genuinely need different keywords for the same idea: CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY in T-SQL versus LATERAL in PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Oracle. See you there.
